δουπῆσαι [to have fallen with a crash] or δεδουπέναι [to have fallen with a crash] are said by the epic poets of those who fell in battle with a crash (of arms): hence Hesychius interprets δέδουπε [has fallen] as τέθνηκεν ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον ἐν πολέμω [has died, for the most part in war], and δεδουπότος [of one who has fallen]: τεθνηκότος, πεπτωκότος [of one who has died, of one who has fallen]. Hence Bernhardy restored δέδουπεν [has fallen] for δέδορκεν [has seen] in fr. 440, about which we have spoken under δέρκομαι [to see].

It is clear that these words are poorly emended. For there is no doubt that the discussion is about the viper that bit Philoctetes. One should write οὐ γὰρ δακών [for not having bitten] (sc. ὁ ὄφις [the snake]) ἀνῆκεν [let go] with G. A. Hirschig in Annot. in Comicos (Trai. ad Rhen. 1849 p. 37), keeping ἀνῆκεν [let go or released], which Valcken. (Diatr. in Eurip. p. 128), not noticing the fault in the preceding word, had changed to ἐνῆκεν [sent in]. He also erred in changing λαβεῖν [to take] to λαβών [having taken]. Correctly, as it seems, Schneidewin in Philologus vol. 4 p. 658, βλάβην [harm], with Reiske leading the way, who had conjectured λώβην ποδός [outrage to the foot].
as someone fears dragons for their children
he will confine the young as a hostile dragon

she dreamed she gave birth to a dragon
having easily cut off the heads of two dragons
a country dragon, a bane to travelers

And from the toil (but it is Wyttenb.) the witness is the Philoctetes of Aeschylus (fr. 248), sufficient: "For the dragon (he says) did not let go, but caused a terrible sharp-toothed growth to take hold of his foot."
